nodes.description: Investigational AAV9-Mpz-GJB1 gene replacement was tested in Gjb1-null mice, using lumbar intrathecal administration before onset at two months and after onset at six months. Compared with mock-vector controls, treatment improved grip strength, conduction velocity, myelin pathology and selected blood biomarkers. Correction was partial; CMAP amplitudes did not improve significantly and late-treatment conduction velocities remained below wild-type values. Schwann-cell-specific expression does not establish treatment of CNS episodes. These experiments provide no human efficacy or safety result.

nodes.description: Cx32 is expressed in oligodendrocytes as well as Schwann cells. nodes.description: In CMTX1, pathogenic GJB1 variants reduce normal Cx32 function in myelinating Schwann cells. Some variants prevent protein expression or membrane trafficking; others form channels with altered gating or permeability. Cx32 normally contributes to reflexive junctions between cytoplasmic layers of the same Schwann cell. Loss of Cx32 does not establish loss of every radial diffusion route or direct axon-to-glial metabolite transfer.

nodes.description: Patient-derived CMTX3 iPSCs and caudal neuroepithelial progenitors show reduced SOX3 abundance. NanoString detected an approximately 5.7-fold iPSC RNA reduction. In progenitors from two patients and three controls, DESeq2 detected approximately 3.89-fold lower RNA; edgeR narrowly missed its significance threshold (FDR 0.0506). Proteomics in three patient and three control progenitor lines independently detected reduced SOX3 protein. Later differentiation stages did not show significant NanoString differences. SOX3 is a leading candidate regulatory target, not an established causal CMT gene: the study lacked isogenic controls and functional rescue, patient lines were related, and neuronal or glial dysfunction from altered SOX3 was not demonstrated. The specific regulatory interaction and expression outside the assayed developmental stages remain unresolved.

nodes.description: GJB1-associated stroke-like episodes are generally self-limited and managed supportively. Recognition of this syndrome does not establish the cause of a new acute neurological presentation; the reported cases included assessment for alternative causes. Counseling includes avoidance of known precipitants where feasible: hyperventilation or exertion, re-acclimatization after returning from high altitude, fever, head trauma and minor infections. GeneReviews states that this may reduce episodes, but advice must be balanced with quality of life; it is not evidence that blanket exercise restriction prevents events.
